--- title: "R3: Read and write data in R" date: "August 16, 2024" date-modified: "2026-11-03 (17:52 h)" categories: - Input - Output - Read - Write - Path - Working Directory engine: knitr format: html page-layout: full filters: - webr toc: true toc-location: left toc-depth: 3 number-sections: true code-overflow: wrap link-external-icon: true link-external-newwindow: true --- ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: # [Working directory and file paths in R]{style="color:darkblue"} When working with R, we often need to read data from files and write results back to disk. These files can be simple text files, comma-separated tables, spreadsheet exports (e.g. MS Excel files), or more specialised formats used in biological data analysis. Before reading or writing files, R needs to know **where to look for them**. By default, R reads and writes files in the current *working directory (wd)*. You can think of the working directory as the folder where R is currently "standing". The *wd* is indicated in the Console panel, as you can see below in a screenshot of my RStudio screen right now. ![](images/console.png){width="545"} Note that the abbreviation `~` stands for your home directory. For example, this may correspond to `/Users/modesto` in macOS, `/home/modesto` in Linux, or `C:/Users/your_user_name` in Windows. The functions `getwd()` and `setwd()` allow you to check and change the *wd*. Try the examples below and pay attention to the output. Remember that you can write `?getwd()` or `?setwd()` for help. ::: callout-warning ## File paths in different operating systems File paths are written differently depending on the operating system. Linux and macOS use forward slashes (`/`), whereas Windows usually displays paths with backslashes (`\`). In R, however, it is safer and simpler to write Windows paths using forward slashes (`/`) or double backslashes (`\\`), because a single backslash has a special meaning inside character strings. For example, this Windows path: ``` text C:\Users\Ana\Documents\HPBBM2025\data ``` can be written in R as: ``` r "C:/Users/Ana/Documents/HPBBM2025/data" ``` or as: ``` r "C:\\Users\\Ana\\Documents\\HPBBM2025\\data" ``` ::: The following example was generated in a Windows 11 computer. However, unless otherwise indicated, most of the examples and exercises in this site were generated under macOS or Ubuntu and should be adapted if you want to try them out in Windows. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Windows example # First, check where R is currently looking for files. # This is useful before reading or writing any file. getwd() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "C:/Users/MR.5052598/OneDrive - UAM/Documentos/GitHub/r4biochemists.github.io" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Now we change the working directory to an existing folder. # Notice that, even in Windows, we use forward slashes (/). setwd("C:/Users/MR.5052598") getwd() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "C:/Users/MR.5052598" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Intentional mistake 1: typo in the folder name. # "Documnts" does not exist, so setwd() should return an error. # This is a common source of problems when file paths are typed manually. setwd("C:/Users/MR.5052598/Documnts") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `setwd()`: ! no es posible cambiar el directorio de trabajo ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Intentional mistake 2: invalid/unwanted character at the end of the path. # The extra ">" makes the path different from the real folder name. # This is useful to show that file paths must match exactly. setwd("C:/Users/MR.5052598/Documents") # If the previous command worked, this would show the new working directory. # Since the line above is intentionally wrong, this helps students see that # the working directory has not changed as expected. getwd() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "C:/Users/MR.5052598/Documents" ``` ::: ::: In RStudio, the *default working directory* can be set from the **Tools \> Global Options** menu. You can also change the *wd* for your session in **Session \> Set Working Directory**, selecting the folder of the source file, the current file location, or a folder selected in the Files panel. ::: callout-tip ## Wouldn't it be great if you didn't have to manually set the working directory every time? If setting the working directory feels annoying or confusing, you can avoid it by using an [R Project](r7.html#rprojects) in RStudio, as explained in Lesson R7. R Projects automatically manage the working directory for you, making your workflow smoother and more reproducible. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## [Quick exercise (I): file paths in Windows]{style="color:darkseagreen"} Imagine that your course data folder is located here in Windows: ``` text C:\Users\Ana\Documents\HPBBM2025\data ``` Which path is safest and simplest to use in R? **Select the right answer**
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## [Quick exercise (II): working directory]{style="color:darkseagreen"} Let's see if you understood. Consider the following tree of directories. ![](images/tree.png){width="279"} How would you change the *wd* to the folder `HPBBM2023/data`? You can also try this with your own computer and your own directory tree. **Select the right answer**
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## [Quick exercise (III): relative paths]{style="color:darkseagreen"} Suppose your current working directory is: ``` text HPBBM2025/ ``` and inside it you have this folder structure: ``` text HPBBM2025/ ├── data/ │ └── small_matrix.csv ├── scripts/ └── results/ ``` Which command reads `small_matrix.csv` without changing the working directory? **Select the right answer**
------------------------------------------------------------------------ # [Reading & writing data in R]{style="color:darkblue"} A common first step in data analysis is importing a file into R. In this lesson, we will focus on tabular text files, such as `.txt` or `.csv` files. These files store data in rows and columns, using a separator character to divide the fields. The base R function `read.table()` is a flexible function for reading tabular data. Several commonly used functions, such as `read.csv()` and `read.csv2()`, are convenient wrappers around `read.table()` with different default options. For example: - `read.table()` is general and flexible, but often requires specifying arguments such as `sep`, `header` or `dec`. - `read.csv()` is designed for comma-separated files, usually using `,` as field separator and `.` as decimal separator. - `read.csv2()` is common in European spreadsheet exports, usually using `;` as field separator and `,` as decimal separator. ## [Quick exercise (IV): choosing an import function]{style="color:darkseagreen"} You have a file named `measurements.csv` with the following structure: ``` text sample,temperature,pH A,37.0,7.2 B,36.5,7.4 C,38.1,7.1 ``` Which function would be the simplest first choice to import this file? **Select the right answer** ## [Quick exercise (V): comma or semicolon?]{style="color:darkseagreen"} A file exported from a spreadsheet program looks like this: ``` text sample;temperature;pH A;37,0;7,2 B;36,5;7,4 C;38,1;7,1 ``` Which function is most appropriate as a first attempt? **Select the right answer** ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## [Reading data example]{style="color:darkblue"} In the following example, we read a file called [*small_matrix.csv*](data/small_matrix.csv), located in the [`data`](https://github.com/r4biochemists/r4biochemists.github.io/tree/main/data) folder. Although the file contains numerical values arranged like a matrix, `read.table()` imports it as a *data frame*. A data frame is a very useful structure for tabular data, but some matrix-specific functions may require explicitly converting it into a matrix with `as.matrix()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sm <- read.table("small_matrix.csv", sep=",") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning in file(file, "rt"): no fue posible abrir el archivo 'small_matrix.csv': No such file or directory ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `file()`: ! no se puede abrir la conexión ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Intentional mistake: we tried to read the file as if it were located # directly in the working directory. # However, the file is actually inside the data/ folder. # This should return an error such as "cannot open the connection". # # When a file cannot be found, the first useful diagnostic step is # to check the working directory. getwd() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "C:/Users/MR.5052598/OneDrive - UAM/Documentos/GitHub/r4biochemists.github.io" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Correct version: include the relative path from the working directory # to the file. Here, the file is inside the data/ folder. sm <- read.table("data/small_matrix.csv", sep=",") # Print the object to inspect the imported table. sm ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` V1 V2 V3 1 2 7 19 2 22 10 80 3 18 3 13 4 25 6 16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Important point: read.table() imports tabular data as a data frame, # even if all values are numeric. is.matrix(sm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Some functions, such as t(), may work because R can coerce the object # to a matrix when possible. t(sm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] V1 2 22 18 25 V2 7 10 3 6 V3 19 80 13 16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Arithmetic operations may also work if all columns are numeric. sm * 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` V1 V2 V3 1 6 21 57 2 66 30 240 3 54 9 39 4 75 18 48 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Intentional problem: diag() expects a matrix-like object. # Depending on the object structure, this may fail or behave unexpectedly. diag(sm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `diag()`: ! 'list' object cannot be coerced to type 'double' ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Correct approach: explicitly convert the data frame into a matrix. diag(as.matrix(sm)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 10 13 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Same idea with heatmap(): it is a matrix-oriented function. # The first call is intentionally included to show what happens if we # pass a data frame directly. heatmap(sm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `heatmap()`: ! 'x' must be a numeric matrix ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Correct approach: convert the data frame explicitly. heatmap(as.matrix(sm)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](r3_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## [Quick exercise (VI): data frame or matrix?]{style="color:darkseagreen"} After importing a numerical table with `read.table()`, you obtain an object called `sm`. Which command checks whether `sm` is a matrix? **Select the right answer** Which command converts `sm` into a matrix? **Select the right answer** ::: callout-tip Note that `read.table()` and its wrappers `read.csv()` or `read.csv2()` are mostly used for reading data frames. If you want to read text files, like in the case of biological sequences, you can use other functions, such as `readLines()`, described in [Lesson R8](r9.html). ::: ## [Writing tables and saving R objects]{style="color:darkblue"} Once you have created or modified an object in R, you may want to save it. There are two common situations: 1. **Saving a table as a text file**, so that it can be opened by other programs. 2. **Saving R objects**, so that they can be loaded again in R with their structure preserved. For tables, we can use functions such as `write.table()`, `write.csv()` or `write.csv2()`. For R objects, we can use `save()`, `load()`, `saveRDS()` or `readRDS()`. You can write any data object as a binary data file or as a text file. Compare the different files saved in the code below. ::: {#save1} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Create two simple example objects. vector <- c(1:5) vector2 <- c(3, 5:13) # write() writes a simple vector to a text file. # This is useful for simple objects, but not usually the best option # for complete data frames. write(vector2,file="data/vector2.txt") # write.table() writes a tabular object to a text file. # Intentional issue for discussion: by default, write.table() writes # row names and column names and uses spaces as separator. # Open the resulting file and compare it with sm2.csv below. write.table(sm,"data/sm.csv") # Here we explicitly control the output: # - row.names = FALSE avoids saving row numbers as an extra column. # - col.names = FALSE avoids saving column names. # - sep = "," creates comma-separated values. write.table(sm,"data/sm2.csv", row.names = FALSE, col.names=FALSE, sep=",") # save() stores one or more R objects in a binary RData file. # When loaded again, the original object names will be restored. save(vector, vector2,file="data/vector2.Rdata") # save.image() stores the whole current workspace. # This is useful to know, but in reproducible analyses it is usually # better to save scripts and selected objects explicitly. save.image(file='data/myEnvironment.RData') ``` ::: ::: {#load} ::: Data files in `RData` format can be opened from the *Environment* tab or with the `load()` function. To check that it was correctly loaded, we can remove it before loading with the `rm()` function. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Remove the objects from the Global Environment in our RStudio session. # This allows us to check whether load() really restores them. rm(vector) rm(vector2) # load() restores the object names that were saved in the RData file. # Notice that we do not choose new names here. load("data/vector2.Rdata") # Check that the objects are available again. vector ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 4 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} vector2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 5 6 7 8 9 10 11 12 13 ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-caution Note that if you save your data with `save()`, it cannot be restored under a different name. The original object names are automatically used. If you want to save one object and restore it with a different name, use the functions `saveRDS()` and `readRDS()`. ::: ## [Quick exercise (VII): `save()` or `saveRDS()`?]{style="color:darkseagreen"} You want to save a single object called `sm`, and later load it under a different name, for example `my_matrix`. Which pair of functions is most appropriate? **Select the right answer** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # saveRDS() saves a single R object. # Unlike save(), it does not force us to restore the object with its # original name. saveRDS(sm, file = "data/sm.rds") # readRDS() returns the saved object, so we can assign it to any name. # Here we deliberately use a new name. my_matrix <- readRDS("data/sm.rds") ``` ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## [Quick exercise (VIII)]{style="color:darkseagreen"} We are using the same directory tree. Your *wd* is `HPBBM2022/data` and you need to save a data frame named `table1` as `table1.csv` in the folder `HPBBM2023/data` using `;` as separator. How would you do it *without changing* the working directory? Try it also with your own computer. **Select the right answer**
------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: callout-note # Interactive data input & output in R You will almost always import your working data from a file. However, especially if you are working with very small datasets, it is also possible to add your data interactively directly in the console, as you did in some of the examples before. You can also define your objects and enter your data interactively using the `scan()` and `readline()` functions, as in the examples below. For output, you can simply call the object by its name or use the `print()` function, which displays the contents of the object on the screen. You can try the following code.[^1] ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # This chunk is not evaluated when the page is rendered because these # functions require interactive input from the user. # scan(n = 4) asks the user to enter exactly four values. vector <- scan(n=4) # scan() without n keeps reading values until the user stops input. vector2 <- scan() # readline() reads one line of text from the console. str <- readline() # Calling an object name prints the object. vector # print() makes the output explicit. This is useful inside functions # or scripts where you want to control what is displayed. print(vector2) print(str) # edit() opens an interactive editor for the object. # This is useful to know, but it is not usually recommended in # reproducible scripts because manual edits are not recorded as code. edit(str) ``` ::: Although seldom used, you can also edit the contents of your objects using the function `edit()`. This function can be used to edit different objects, including vectors, strings, matrices or data frames. macOS users may need to install [XQuartz X11](https://www.xquartz.org/) tool. ::: [^1]: Since it is interactive, we cannot run it when we render the source file into a static web page. This can be prevented in Markdown/Quarto with the option `eval: false` in the chunk. # [Basic Data Management in R]{style="color:darkblue"} Now we are going to import and explore an example dataset containing metadata from an Illumina sequencing project of pathogenic *E. coli* strains (Flament-Simon et al. 2020, ). However, for didactic purposes, the original data have been simplified and manipulated and the attached datasets do not fully correspond to the actual data. You can find the table in the [`data`](https://github.com/r4biochemists/r4biochemists.github.io/tree/main/data) folder or download it here: [coli_genomes.csv](data/coli_genomes.csv). ## Open and explore a data frame As you can see in the R help, the function `read.table()` has several default options, such as `header = FALSE`. When you have a spreadsheet export file where fields are divided by commas or semicolons, you can use `read.csv()` or `read.csv2()` instead of writing all the arguments manually in `read.table()`. For Spaniards, there is also `read.csv2()`, which uses a comma for the decimal point and a semicolon for the separator. These functions are wrappers of `read.table()` with custom default options. Likewise, there are `write.csv()` and `write.csv2()`, which are wrappers of `write.table()`. Before analysing a dataset, it is important to inspect it. A quick first exploration usually includes checking: - the first and last rows, - the number of rows and columns, - the variable names, - the type of each variable, - whether some values may need cleaning. The following commands are a useful first checklist when opening a new table in R. They also illustrate several ways to open a table, including some common mistakes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Note differences between read.table(), read.csv() and read.csv2(). # Intentional mistake / incomplete import: # read.table() assumes header = FALSE and uses whitespace as separator by default. # Our file is semicolon-separated and has a header line, so the result will not # be imported as intended. coli_genomes <- read.table(file = "data/coli_genomes.csv") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error in `scan()`: ! line 2 did not have 11 elements ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(coli_genomes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ``` Error: ! objeto 'coli_genomes' no encontrado ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Better: here we specify the separator, decimal character and header. # This is the explicit read.table() version. coli_genomes <- read.table(file = "data/coli_genomes.csv", sep=";", dec=".", header=TRUE) head(coli_genomes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Strain Biosample Year.of.isolation Source Phylogroup Serotype Clonotype 1 LREC237 SAMN14278613 NA Human D ONT:H28 CH23-331 2 LREC239 SAMN14278614 2010 Human C O153:H19 CH4-25 3 LREC240 SAMN14278615 2008 Human B1 O76:H30 CH29-38 4 LREC241 SAMN14278616 NA Human A O78:H11 CH11-41 5 LREC242 SAMN14278617 2011 Porcine A ONT:HNM CH7-54 6 LREC243 SAMN14278618 2007 Porcine A O9:H37 CH7-31 Sequence.Type VF No..Plasmids kmer Contigs N50 longest.contig..bp. 1 ST524 18 3 117 223 272287 662555 2 ST88 14 3 117 159 323172 760527 3 ST156 10 2 89 114 270767 738861 4 ST48 5 3 117 212 112160 285056 5 ST746 5 9 89 320 45936 128053 6 ST3011 7 3 93 158 106897 369508 total.assembled.bp contigs...1kb 1 5341632 74 2 5415613 57 3 4875343 47 4 5167401 101 5 4858138 212 6 4638334 93 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Intentional mistake / wrong default for this file: # read.csv() assumes comma-separated values. If the file actually uses semicolons, # the table will not be split into the expected columns. coli_genomes <- read.csv(file = "data/coli_genomes.csv") head(coli_genomes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Strain.Biosample.Year.of.isolation.Source.Phylogroup.Serotype.Clonotype.Sequence.Type.VF.No..Plasmids.kmer.Contigs.N50.longest.contig..bp..total.assembled.bp.contigs...1kb 1 LREC237;SAMN14278613;NA;Human ;D;ONT:H28;CH23-331;ST524;18;3;117;223;272287;662555;5341632;74 2 LREC239;SAMN14278614;2010;Human ;C;O153:H19;CH4-25;ST88;14;3;117;159;323172;760527;5415613;57 3 LREC240;SAMN14278615;2008;Human ;B1;O76:H30;CH29-38;ST156;10;2;89;114;270767;738861;4875343;47 4 LREC241;SAMN14278616;NA;Human;A;O78:H11;CH11-41;ST48;5;3;117;212;112160;285056;5167401;101 5 LREC242;SAMN14278617;2011;Porcine ;A;ONT:HNM;CH7-54;ST746;5;9;89;320;45936;128053;4858138;212 6 LREC243;SAMN14278618;2007;Porcine ;A;O9:H37;CH7-31;ST3011;7;3;93;158;106897;369508;4638334;93 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Better than the previous line: we still use read.csv(), but we manually set # sep = ";". This shows that wrappers can be customised. coli_genomes <- read.csv(file = "data/coli_genomes.csv", sep=";") head(coli_genomes) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Strain Biosample Year.of.isolation Source Phylogroup Serotype Clonotype 1 LREC237 SAMN14278613 NA Human D ONT:H28 CH23-331 2 LREC239 SAMN14278614 2010 Human C O153:H19 CH4-25 3 LREC240 SAMN14278615 2008 Human B1 O76:H30 CH29-38 4 LREC241 SAMN14278616 NA Human A O78:H11 CH11-41 5 LREC242 SAMN14278617 2011 Porcine A ONT:HNM CH7-54 6 LREC243 SAMN14278618 2007 Porcine A O9:H37 CH7-31 Sequence.Type VF No..Plasmids kmer Contigs N50 longest.contig..bp. 1 ST524 18 3 117 223 272287 662555 2 ST88 14 3 117 159 323172 760527 3 ST156 10 2 89 114 270767 738861 4 ST48 5 3 117 212 112160 285056 5 ST746 5 9 89 320 45936 128053 6 ST3011 7 3 93 158 106897 369508 total.assembled.bp contigs...1kb 1 5341632 74 2 5415613 57 3 4875343 47 4 5167401 101 5 4858138 212 6 4638334 93 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # In R, missing values are represented as `NA`, which means "not available". Missing values affect many calculations. For example, if a vector contains at least one `NA`, functions such as `mean()` will usually return `NA` unless we explicitly ask R to remove missing values.
